extracted.intended_audience: students of journalism and young newspaper reporters
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for reporting and writing newspaper news stories, including classification of types, news values, structure (leads/body), style, gathering methods, and analysis questions for students and reporters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of newspaper contents
rubrics_metrics.description: Contents of a typical daily newspaper may be grouped in seven classes: (1) news stories; (2) special feature articles; (3) editorials; (4) dramatic, musical, and literary criticism; (5) practical advice and useful information; (6) humorous matter; (7) fiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish journalistic types (first four) from other contents; use classification to choose appropriate methods and tone for each class.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of news story / news
rubrics_metrics.description: News stories present (1) timely events of interest and significance to readers, and (2) timely incidents of little or no news value that are made entertaining by the manner in which they are presented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether material is timely and interesting to readers; consider whether an item is spot news or later 'detail' material deserving feature treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spot news vs detail/situation material
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between 'spot news' (news of events when they occur) and 'detail' or 'situation' material presented later as special correspondence or feature articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose immediate summary treatment for spot news; use elaboration and contextualization for situation material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special feature article criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Special feature articles are detailed presentations of (1) matters of recent news that warrant elaboration, (2) timely topics not directly connected with the news of the day, (3) subjects of interest that are neither timely nor connected with current events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Feature articles are informative, generally longer, often in magazine sections; length and detail depend on interest and warrant for elaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial purpose and distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorials aim to interpret news and current issues, to discuss matters of general interest, and to persuade readers to act according to the convictions created; this differentiates editorials from news stories and special features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate reporting with editorializing; the intention to persuade is the hallmark of editorial writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organization of news gathering: local vs telegraph
rubrics_metrics.description: From an organizational point of view news is divided into (1) local news gathered by reporters under the city editor, and (2) telegraph news (non-local) coming by telegraph, long-distance telephone, cable, or mail, whether by a paper's correspondents or by news associations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand workflows and responsibilities; know whether material is local (use local sources/angles) or telegraph/association copy (check editing conventions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Speed and workflow in writing
rubrics_metrics.description: After obtaining news the reporter must write rapidly, often under direction of the city editor; sometimes reporters telephone facts to rewrite men or send copy by messenger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Work quickly but accurately; be prepared for rewrite and editorial changes; anticipate the need to supply clear facts for others to shape into a story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions affecting news writing
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure and style of news stories are determined by (1) the conditions under which they are written, (2) the character of the readers, (3) the conditions under which newspapers are read, (4) the typographical form of newspapers, and (5) popular taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust writing to production pressures, readership level, reading habits, column widths, and prevailing tastes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness
rubrics_metrics.description: Conciseness requires that needless words be omitted, that only such details be given as are necessary for effective presentation of the subject, and that the length of the story be proportionate to the importance of the material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Boil it down’ and ‘Cut it to the bone’ are constant admonitions; conciseness does not require a bald style — clarity and attractiveness may remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearness / simplicity of diction
rubrics_metrics.description: Clearness is secured by comparative simplicity of diction, of sentence construction, and of paragraph structure; learned diction, elaborate figures, and involved sentences have no place in newspaper writing intended to appeal to all classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple, direct language; avoid technical or learned words unless fully explained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation to readership (comparative simplicity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The style of writing is generally adapted to readers of limited education as well as the well educated; comparative simplicity of expression is the rule in newspaper writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write for rapid, broad readership; avoid elitist language and constructions that slow reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ease of rapid reading (emphasis by initial position)
rubrics_metrics.description: Important details are placed at the beginning of paragraphs and sentences to catch the eye at once; this initial-position emphasis is a distinctive characteristic of newspaper writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place the most significant points early in sentences and paragraphs to facilitate skimming and rapid comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attractiveness and use of literary devices
rubrics_metrics.description: To satisfy popular taste newspaper writing must be interesting in form and style; papers sometimes adopt devices of fiction for effect, and use typographical means (boxes, bold-face) for emphasis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use literary devices sparingly and ethically; avoid confusing fiction techniques with fabricated facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Summary lead (what it must answer)
rubrics_metrics.description: The informative story usually begins with a summary lead that answers Who? What? Where? When? Why? How? The summary lead includes: (1) the persons, (2) the event, (3) the place, (4) the time, (5) the cause, (6) the significant circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the lead supplies essential facts; any of these elements may be 'featured' depending on importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature/human-interest lead alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: The story of entertainment or appeal usually avoids the summary lead and begins in one of the ways common to fictitious narratives; human-interest or feature stories resemble short stories in beginning and suspense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use non-summary openings for feature pieces where sustaining interest and suspense is primary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure of the body: logical order and repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: In the body of the story the details follow a logical order; arrangement in narrative stories is usually chronological. Only such details summarized in the lead are repeated as needed for clearness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize body material for clarity; avoid unnecessary repetition but round out stories where helpful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of discourse in news
rubrics_metrics.description: News stories in method are (1) narrative, (2) descriptive, (3) expository, or any combination of these three forms of discourse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose form(s) appropriate to the material — e.g., narrative for incidents, descriptive for scenes, expository to explain causes or summarize reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary style elements and qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Style concerns paragraphs, sentences, words; and qualities such as clearness, force, animation, humor, pathos, taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze paragraph/sentence length, unity, coherence, and emphasis; cultivate appropriate tone (humor without vulgarity, pathos without offensiveness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Paragraph length and column effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of narrow columns the newspaper paragraph must be comparatively short; the typical newspaper paragraph contains from 35 to 75 words (versus 150–250 in ordinary prose).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep paragraphs short to avoid heavy appearance and to aid rapid reading; adapt to column width (about six words per average line).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence construction and avoidance of involved periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Involved constructions, long periodic sentences, and similar rhetorical devices have no place in journalistic writing because they tend to prevent rapid reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer loose, direct sentence structures that place emphasis early; avoid complex, periodic syntax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word choice and technical language
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific words in original combinations are always preferable to colorless, general terms and trite phrases. Technical, scientific, and learned words should be avoided unless fully explained. Slang and colloquial expressions may be used when the tone of the story justifies them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor vivid, precise wording; explain necessary technical terms; use slang only where appropriate and tasteful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description: suggestive vs detailed
rubrics_metrics.description: Description in news stories may be either suggestive or detailed; lack of space usually requires suggestive touches, while longer stories may allow detailed description aimed to convey impressions of sights and sounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose descriptive depth based on space and significance; make descriptions convey the reporter's impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exposition: simplicity and lucidity
rubrics_metrics.description: When situations must be made clear by explaining motives, causes, results, and other phases of the news, exposition should always be as simple and lucid as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain complex matters plainly; avoid jargon and convoluted explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typographical style and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: Peculiarities of typographical style (abbreviation, capitalization, hyphenation, numerical figures) differ by paper, but consistency must be maintained. Use of boxes, bold-face, methods for lists (dead/injured), and market/score formats should be noted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the paper's house style consistently; use typographical emphasis where appropriate to highlight facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: News values (what makes news)
rubrics_metrics.description: News values are based largely on the reader's interest in (1) timely matters, (2) extraordinary events and circumstances, (3) struggles for supremacy in politics/business/sports, (4) matters involving property, life, and welfare, (5) children, (6) animals, (7) hobbies and amusements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge newsworthiness by these categories when deciding space and prominence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of reader interest factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of reader's interest is proportionate to (1) familiarity with persons/places/things involved, (2) importance/prominence of these persons/places/things, (3) closeness of their relation to the reader's personal affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Localize telegraph or general news by bringing out aspects that relate to the paper's readers to increase interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local vs general news evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: The distinction between local news and general news grows out of the greater interest in persons and places that readers know and in matters closely related to their business and home; interest varies inversely with distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize local ends in general news to raise its value to the paper's audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of news (attribution and inference)
rubrics_metrics.description: From details of a story one can often infer sources: public and private records, reports, officials, eye-witnesses, etc.; these sources should be noted carefully for use in reporting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite or note likely sources; compile lists of sources for recurring story types (crime, fires, accidents).

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of news gathering (evidence in the story)
rubrics_metrics.description: How the details were obtained (interviews, documents, eyewitness accounts) may often be inferred; the student should note evidence of methods used and any indications of missing important details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about methods when necessary; ensure thoroughness and check for gaps the story's form reveals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose, fairness, and bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Every news story should present details as accurately and as completely as the significance warrants. Embellishment with fictitious details, distortion, or suppression to accomplish some end is opposed to the fundamental purpose of the newspaper. The writer’s attitude influences whether a story has constructive or destructive effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the story is fair and unbiased; avoid suppression or coloring to fit policy; be mindful of the story's social impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive journalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Constructive stories emphasize causes, responsibility, frequency of occurrences to impress on readers the importance of preventive measures and to substitute suggestions that tend to prevent similar acts; they may deliberately present news to have a wholesome effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adopting constructive aims, present accurate facts while emphasizing aspects that promote public welfare; avoid sensationalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensationalism and its critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Some newspapers give prominence to sensational, ghastly, and scandalous phases because they appeal to morbid interest; critics argue such treatment sacrifices social responsibility and is not justified by 'giving the public what it wants.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resist gratuitous sensationalism; weigh public interest against potential harmful effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of informative stories (pure vs constructive)
rubrics_metrics.description: The informative news story may be (1) purely informative — records facts for rapid grasping, usually with a summary lead; or (2) constructive — presents facts to produce a wholesome effect on readers and may or may not use a summary lead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to aim merely to inform or to inform with a constructive purpose; let that decision shape emphasis and length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feature (entertaining) story criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Entertainment/feature stories contain little or no news; interest is entirely in the manner of telling. The literary ability of the writer is tested to sustain the reader’s interest; length depends on success in sustaining interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply fiction techniques ethically; ensure the story's truthfulness even when using narrative devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis checklist / methods of analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: In studying a news story consider: (1) the value of the news; (2) the sources; (3) the methods of obtaining it; (4) the purpose of the story; (5) the type of story; (6) the structure; (7) the literary style; (8) the typographical style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the provided outline of questions (e.g., 'In what paper was the story published?', 'Is the story fair and unbiased?', 'Is there a summary lead?', etc.) to evaluate stories systematically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lead elements that may be 'featured'
rubrics_metrics.description: Any one of the elements of the summary lead (persons, event, place, time, cause, significant circumstances) may be 'featured' in the place of prominence at the beginning of the story; time and place are seldom featured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select which element to emphasize in the lead according to reader interest and the story's purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ending and rounding out stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Although it is well to round out stories in the last paragraph, the ending does not receive as much attention as in other prose because make-up exigencies often necessitate cutting off the last paragraph or two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a usable ending but write expecting possible truncation; prioritize conveying the essential facts earlier.
